Yet other orders, however, are rooted in broadly worded statutes by 
which Congress has sometimes delegated administrative authority directly 
to presidents. These directives may well bind the public and appear, as do 
many agency regulations, in circumstances where legislation would have 
been equally appropriate. In 1943, President Roosevelt, without citing 
specific statutory authority, but presumably resting on the federal 
government’s broad discretion in procurement, required “[a] 11 contracting 
agencies of the Government of the United States” to include provisions in 
every contract “obligating the contractor not to discriminate against any 
employee or applicant for employment because of race, creed, color, or 
national origin and requiring him to include a similar provision in all 
subcontracts.” Exec. Order No. 9,346, 8 Fed. Reg. 7183 (1943). Congress’s 
enactment in 1949 of broad presidential authority to regulate government 
property and procurement via the Federal Property and Administrative 
Services Act (FPASA), Pub. 81-152, 63 Stat. 377, 40 U.S.C. § 121, 
emboldened yet further antidiscrimination regulation by executive order. 
President Kennedy issued a far-reaching order in 1962 on 
nondiscrimination in housing owned, operated, or financed by the federal 
government. Exec. Order No. 11,063, 27 Fed. Reg. 11527 (1962). 
Subsequent presidents have revised the employment nondiscrimination 
obhgations of federal contractors, for example, to include gender. Exec. 
Order No. 11,375, 32 Fed. Reg. 14303 (1967), and later gender identity. 
Exec. Order No. 13,672, 79 Fed. Reg. 42791 (2014). As we noted in Chapter 
2, the executive order has also been used as a device to institute wage and 
price controls through the government’s power of procurement and its use 
of pubhcity. The courts’ receptivity has been mixed, however, with regard 
to the presidential use of broadly defined statutory procurement powers to 
implement social policy through executive orders. Compare Bradford v. 
U.S, Dep't of Lab., 101 F.4th 707, 715 (10th Cir. 2024) (denying injunction 
against implementation of executive order imposing $15.00 minimum wage 
for employees of federal contractors) and Contractors Ass'n of E, 
Pennsylvania v. Sec^y of Labor, 442 F.2d 159 (3d Cir.), cert, denied, 404 U.S. 
854 (1971) (upholding executive order imposing affirmative action 
requirements on federal contractors), with Chamber of Commerce of the 
United States of America v, Reich, 83 F.3d 439 (D.C. Cir. 1996) 
(invahdating Executive Order authorizing Secretary of Labor to disqualify 
from certain federal contracts employers who hire permanent replacement 
workers during a lawful strike).
